source.title: Regularising Fisher Information Improves Cross-lingual Generalisation

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a different measured property, Fisher information trace, tracks generalization in multilingual fine-tuning.
record.gate_note: Reports two correlations involving Fisher information trace and validation performance. It does not test the claim versions’ specific architectures, optimizers, batch sizes, dropout effects, memorization capacity, or example-removal effects.
record.test_reason: The study measures Fisher-trace correlations with multilingual BERT validation accuracy and transfer gains. It does not test any listed version. In particular, Fisher trace is not magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, and validation accuracy or transfer gain is not the training–test gap required by V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors describe preliminary correlations between smaller Fisher trace and validation performance or subsequent target-language fine-tuning gains, and report that direct Fisher penalties achieve results similar to subword consistency regularization. They propose confirmation on more datasets.
record.recipe_differences: Fine-tuning multilingual BERT for cross-lingual transfer; measures Fisher trace rather than magnitude-aware weight perturbation sharpness.
record.method_sensitivity: Consistency-loss and Fisher-penalty weights varied in the XNLI experiment; target language varied in PAWS-X.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report that smaller final Fisher trace accompanies higher English validation accuracy on a 20,000-example XNLI subset and larger target-language fine-tuning gains on PAWS-X.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested multilingual BERT fine-tuning settings, smaller Fisher information trace correlates with better validation performance and greater benefit from subsequent target-language fine-tuning.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 1st Workshop on Multilingual Representation Learning (MRL), 2021
record.problems: The XNLI experiment uses a 20k-example subset chosen due to compute constraints. Results are presented as plots and qualitative correlations, without numerical correlation values or uncertainty estimates. The authors describe the results as preliminary.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the corresponding natural-label and random-label held-out accuracies.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed to fit the training data.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove them.
Dropout effects on held-out error across data sizes and regularization settings.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus training–test gaps among similarly fitted convolutional networks, including comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The authors interpret small Fisher trace as flatter minima, but this does not establish the specific sharpness–generalization-gap relationship in V7. No numerical correlation coefficients or uncertainty estimates are supplied.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and tuning conditions.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its comparison with norm- and margin-based measures, and the specified convolutional-family conditions.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

rows.check: The reported correlation is an unrelated finding, not an observed instance of V7. The experiment measures Fisher trace and English validation accuracy, without magnitude-aware perturbations, training–test gaps, or comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures. Numerical points cannot be recovered from the supplied figure text.
